newsitem.title: JAPAN: Costly Japan gas pipeline plan gets mixed review.
newsitem.headline: Costly Japan gas pipeline plan gets mixed review.

text.p: A new master plan for a pipeline network that would both import natural gas and distribute it within Japan adds to the ongoing debate on how the island nation should satisfy its growing appetite for energy.
But the plan won't go far unless someone is willing to foot the roughly $30-billion bill, industry sources say.

Drafted by the privately run National Pipeline Research Society of Japan (NPRSJ), the latest plan offers one option on how to supply imported natural gas by trunk pipeline from Russia's Far East -- widely seen as a promising future source of natural gas for resource-poor Japan.

The plan's architects say transporting natural gas by pipeline would help cut transportation costs and other accompanying costs, but add that the scheme -- which calls for building two main pipelines at a total cost of 3.5 trillion yen ($30.7 billion) -- will need an operating body prepared to fund and press ahead with the project if it is to move beyond mere blueprint status.
NPRSJ secretary general Kengo Asakura said that was likely to prove difficult.

"Right now there is no specific group in Japan that is working on building a main domestic (natural gas) pipeline, (and) I don't think that any existing entity is capable of handling the programme all by itself," he said.

A Japanese company with oil and gas interests in Russia's Sakhalin Island said the viability of the plan also depended on whether customers wanted to receive the energy in its raw state, as natural gas, or as liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Currently, almost all of the the natural gas Japan consumes is shipped to Japan as LNG, which compared to natural gas, is easier to transport or store.
Japan's domestic natural gas production accounts for less than four percent of annual domestic consumption.
The balance, annual imports which amounted to roughly 44,000 tonnes in fiscal 1995/96 (April/March), makes Japan the world's largest LNG importer by far.

Additional concerns were that Japan's major gas companies would be lukewarm to the idea because an extensive distribution network would pave the way for new entrants into their market, and thereby increase competition.

Gas fields in Russia's Irkutsk in Siberia and Sakhalin Island regions provide a relatively close, and therefore attractive source of energy for Japan, which has had to rely on the Middle East for some 80 percent of its crude oil requirements.
However, there are currently no domestic pipeline networks that can transport the natural gas once it reaches Japan.

NPRSJ's plan calls for two pipelines, one a 2,400-km (1,500 mile) line that would link gas fields in Sakhalin to Japan, and would run from north to southwest mainly following the Sea of Japan coast once it hit Japan's main island. The other, roughly 2,500 km (1,563 mile) in length, would mainly connect Sendai on Japan's Pacific coast and run mostly along the Pacific seaboard.

A Ministry of International Trade and Industry official said that the ministry was following such studies with interest, but that a pipeline project was seen as being largely the domain of the private sector.
Natural gas demand in East Asia is expected to more than double to around 300 billion cubic metres a year by 2010 from the current 140 billion cubic metres, according to the Japan Gas Association.
